limitsWhy.claudeMdLines: The Claude Code documentation's target: files over 200 lines consume more context and may reduce adherence.
limitsWhy.ruleLines: A rules file is read like a CLAUDE.md; the same target keeps each one readable whole.
limitsWhy.ruleChars: A scoped rule loads on demand and is cut at 40,000 characters on a 200K context window; a file under that loads whole for everyone.
limitsWhy.areaChars: The scoped rules of one area load together when a file there is touched; 40,000 characters is about 10,000 tokens, a cost worth paying on every such turn, and not more.
limitsWhy.unscopedChars: Rules without paths load in every session, so they are the most expensive per character; 10,000 keeps them to the few that really apply everywhere.
limitsWhy.skillLines: The documentation's target for a SKILL.md; reference material goes in files beside it, loaded when needed.
limitsWhy.memoryIndexLines: Only the first 200 lines of MEMORY.md load at a session's start; a line past that is a memory the session never knows it has.
limitsWhy.memoryIndexBytes: Or the first 25 KB, whichever comes first.
limitsWhy.memoryNoteCommits: bowline's own threshold, not a Claude Code limit. A note is read whole whenever it looks relevant, and a finished item needs only a pointer to the record and its last commit, so a note that names ten commits keeps several finished items in full and buries what is still open. Commits, not lines: on the first user's memory, sizes did not tell a log from a long reference note, and the commits did.
limitsWhy.memoryBackupHours: The backup runs after every reply and prints nothing, so a hook that stopped or a push that fails shows nowhere else, and a lost machine loses every note that waits. The hours are bowline's own threshold, not a Claude Code limit: a day is longer than a night without a reply, and short enough that little is at risk; 0 turns the check off.
limitsWhy.onDemandCutoffSmallWindow: A nested CLAUDE.md or a scoped rule is cut here on a 200K context window; Claude gets a note that it may read the rest, and usually does not.
limitsWhy.onDemandCutoffLargeWindow: The same cut on a 1M context window with current models.
limitsWhy.skippedFileBytes: A CLAUDE.md over 4 MiB is skipped entirely.

gateWhy.tokens: A pushed secret cannot be taken back, even after a later commit removes it; the patterns need a token's real length after the prefix so a fake prefix in a test does not stop a commit.
gateWhy.controlBytes: A bell or another control character survives a type check and breaks a terminal or a string.
gateWhy.byteOrderMark: A byte-order mark is invisible, passes the compilers, and breaks the first line of a file or a commit message.
gateWhy.lineEndings: A repository that is LF only keeps diffs honest; a carriage return in one line makes the whole file look changed. Set to any to allow both.
gateWhy.crlfFiles: Windows batch files are the one kind that needs CRLF (cmd's goto misses labels in a long LF-only file), so the carriage-return rule skips files matching these patterns; a .gitattributes line checks them out that way.
gateWhy.nonAscii: warn names characters outside ASCII without stopping the commit; refuse stops it, for a repository whose convention is ASCII only; ignore says nothing. acceptedCharacters lists the exceptions, as characters or as U+XXXX.
gateWhy.neverCommitList: Words that must never be committed, one regular expression per line, kept outside every repository so the repository itself never holds them; the gate reads the file when it exists and says nothing when it does not.

autosplitWhy.enabled: Off by default: a background worker spends tokens and makes a branch, so each repository opts in, in its own .claude/bowline.json, where every contributor sees that it did.
autosplitWhy.deliver: How the result arrives. branch, the default: the two commits wait on their branch for the person to review and cherry-pick. merge: the worker cherry-picks them onto the current branch itself as soon as the split is ready, only onto a clean working tree and only when they apply without a conflict (otherwise the split stays on its branch and the doctor says why), never with a push; the doctor then says what landed until the person runs autosplit done.
autosplitWhy.command: The program that starts a headless Claude Code session: a name on the path or a full path, or a list for a program with its arguments. The worker adds what makes the session unattended: -p, acceptEdits, no permission prompts, an allowlist of tools, a JSON result.
autosplitWhy.maxBudgetUsd: The most one split may spend, passed as --max-budget-usd; a session that reaches it stops, and the split is reported as failed with its log, rather than running on. One turn of the largest model with its system prompt cost about half a dollar when this was measured, and a split with condensing subagents takes dozens.
autosplitWhy.timeoutMinutes: The worker stops the session after this long and reports the split as failed, so a hung session cannot run forever.
autosplitWhy.model: A model for the worker's session, or null for the person's default.
autosplitWhy.args: Extra arguments for the command, for example --plugin-dir with the plugin folder of a clone of bowline on a machine where the plugin is not installed.

crewWhy.activeMinutes: How far back a sign of work counts: a session's start names another session when a transcript of another worktree, or another transcript of this folder, was written within this many minutes, and a running session is told before a prompt when one appears; 0 says nothing at all. It is not a wait: the look happens at once, and half an hour only decides who still counts as at work, which covers a session that is thinking or waiting for a check and forgets one that was closed.
crewWhy.assumeOthers: true, the default: every session's start gets the line about working beside other sessions, whether or not another one is seen, because several sessions in one repository is the usual case and the second may start a minute after the first looked. false gives the line only when another session shows a sign of work.
crewWhy.base: The branch every session pushes to, such as origin/main, which the worktrees and the numbered lists are measured against; null asks git for origin's default branch.
crewWhy.heavy: Regular expressions over a process's command line, for the checks that must not run beside one another on one machine: a test suite, a browser test run, a full build. Each repository names its own, because only it knows them; with none, crew run waits for the turn alone. Name the program as it runs, such as "dotnet(\.exe)?\s+test" or "vitest", and never a server a person keeps running, which would never go quiet.
crewWhy.keepPorts: The ports a person's own servers listen on. crew lists what listens on each and says that it must never be stopped; a session that needs a server takes another port.
crewWhy.numbers: The numbered lists several sessions extend, by name: {"roadmap": {"file": "docs/ROADMAP.md", "pattern": "^(\\d+)\\."}}. The pattern is a regular expression, read line by line, whose first group is the number; without one, a line that starts with a number and a dot, a parenthesis or a colon, after an optional list mark, bold mark or number sign, counts. crew claim <name> --new takes the next free number, and the doctor warns when a number appears twice.
crewWhy.shared: The files every session adds to by the repository's own rule, as paths or patterns from its top: a roadmap, a design document, a changelog. crew lists them apart from the files changed in more than one worktree, because two sessions that both changed one is how the work is meant to go, and a list that names them every time teaches its reader to skip it.
crewWhy.stamps: Files a build writes with the commit it was built from: [{"file": "web/.source-commit", "remake": "npm run stamp"}]. After a rebase every commit has a new name, so the doctor and the check after a rebase warn when a stamp names a commit the branch does not hold, and say the command that remakes it.
crewWhy.waitMinutes: How long crew run waits for a quiet machine before it gives up without running the command; a full test suite of the first repository that used it takes about ten minutes, and two may be ahead.
crewWhy.waitEverySeconds: How often crew run looks again. Listing every process takes about a second on Windows, so a look every quarter of a minute costs little and starts the command soon after the machine goes quiet.
crewWhy.memoryLossDays: How far back in the memory backup's history the doctor looks for lines one session added and another removed; 0 turns the check off. A week is long enough to notice at the next session's start and short enough that the history is read in well under a second.
crewWhy.memoryLossHours: A removed line counts as a loss when another session had added it within this many hours. A note saved whole from an older copy loses what was added since that copy was read, which is hours at most; a curation removes lines that are days or weeks old, and stays silent.
crewWhy.warnBeforeEdit: Before Claude edits a file that another worktree of the repository holds (changed there and not committed, committed there and in neither the pushed branch nor this one, or claimed there as file:<path>), a hook tells Claude which worktree and branch hold it, once per session and file, so that the two sessions agree who changes what before both have built on their own copy. It never blocks the edit, and skips the files of shared, numbers and stamps. false turns it off, for a repository whose worktrees are not sessions.
crewWhy.changedCacheSeconds: How old the record of what every worktree changed (changed.json in the repository's git folder) may be before the hook before an edit has it measured again, in the background. Measuring nineteen worktrees on a slow disk took over two minutes on the first repository that was tried, and an edit must not wait for that; a minute is short enough that a file another session just changed is known by the next edit or the one after.
crewWhy.sayChars: How long what a session says of itself with crew say may be; 0 sets no limit. Six hundred characters hold what is done with its commits, what the session waits on and what it asks, and still let a look at ten worktrees be read at once; a longer one is refused, not cut, because a cut report is the loss this exists to prevent.
crewWhy.claude: The program crew asks for the list of sessions, as `<program> agents --json`: a name on the path or a full path, or a list for a program with its arguments. That list holds every session on the machine, Claude Desktop's included, with its name, its folder, its process and whether it is busy, idle or blocked. It answered in under a second on the first machine tried; only the look asks it, and the hooks read what the last look kept. Where it cannot be asked, a transcript written lately stands for a session and its title line names it.
crewWhy.asksFromReply: true, the default: when a session's reply ends with a question, the Stop hook records that the session waits for the person, and every look shows it first until the person's next prompt in that session. Claude Code lists such a session as plain idle, the same as one that is done; on the day this was built three of them were waiting for the person unseen. Only the reply's last sentence is kept, in the repository's git folder, from the hook's last_assistant_message. false leaves it to the sessions to say so with crew say --asks.
crewWhy.watchSeconds: How often crew watch draws the look again. The sessions and the processes are asked anew at each drawing, which takes a second or two; the worktrees are measured in the background, one measuring after another, because a large repository's take a minute.
crewWhy.pruneHours: How long a worktree must have shown no sign of work before crew prune calls it safe to remove, with everything else it asks: nothing not committed, every commit's change on the pushed branch, no session, process, claim, lock or place in the push queue. A session that thinks over a long check for an hour still counts as there; six hours is past a working morning or afternoon.
crewWhy.slots: How many full checks crew run lets run at once, across every session. A heavy process that no crew run started takes a slot too, so with 1 the turn waits for a quiet machine. Memory decides, more than processors: crew run records the most memory each command took, and the look shows the largest, so choose 2 only when twice the largest is less than what is free while no check runs. A small check (crew run --small) runs beside them whatever this says, one at a time, and every check beside another waits until its own peak is free.
crewWhy.oldUntrackedHours: How long untracked files must have gone unwritten before they stop putting a worktree whose sessions are idle under WAITS FOR YOU. A tool's cache or an editor's settings that git does not ignore stay untracked for weeks, and on 2026-11-22 three such files from October put the first user's main checkout first in the look, as idle with work not committed. Such a worktree is listed under IDLE with how many untracked files it holds and the date of the newest. A change to a tracked file, or an untracked file written within this many hours, is still work that waits. crew prune still refuses every untracked file, because git worktree remove does.
crewWhy.desktop: The folder where Claude Desktop keeps a record of each of its Code sessions, one file per session; null is the app's own folder on this system (claude-code-sessions in %APPDATA%\Claude on Windows, in ~/Library/Application Support/Claude on macOS, in ~/.config/Claude elsewhere), and false reads no record. The record is the only place on the machine that holds a session's id in the app, by which a reply there links the session, and its full title, which claude agents cuts at 50 characters. Of each record only the ids, the title, whether it is archived, its folder, its worktree and its last activity are read.

decisionsWhy.records: The files that record decisions, as paths or patterns from the repository's top: a design document's decisions section, a roadmap, a folder of decision records. bowline decisions find lists them first, apart from every other document. With none named, the documents whose name says so are taken: a roadmap, a design document, a decisions page, a changelog, or a file in a folder named adr or decisions. bowline decisions records prints which files those are.
decisionsWhy.within: A place is listed where every word of the subject appears within this many lines of the others. A sentence in a document is wrapped over two or three lines, so one line alone would miss a decision whose words fall on two; a whole entry would list a roadmap item of three hundred lines for any two common words.
decisionsWhy.shown: How many places each part of the list shows before it counts the rest; --verbose lists every one. The list goes into a session's context, and a subject with fifty places is read from its records first.
decisionsWhy.seconds: How long the search of the files may take before the list says that the documents, tests and code were not searched. On the first repository it was measured on, with about 4,000 tracked files, two plain words took 0.3 seconds once the disk had been read, and a search with a pattern took 81 seconds the first time; a tool call ends after two minutes.
decisionsWhy.atStart: In a repository whose instructions have no section about looking a decision up, a session's start gets one sentence that says what to do before a question goes to the person and names /bowline:decide; false gives none. In the replay of 2026-11-28, with the plugin and no such rule in front of the session, the skill was left unused in 5 of 13 runs; with the rule's text, which names the skill, in none of 10. The sentence carries the rule's main point until the repository has the rule. Tried on live sessions the same day: said last and as a description, 2 of 5 sessions used the skill; said before the line about other sessions and as the action to take, 5 of 5.
decisionsWhy.byReference: A regular expression for an entry that approves a number of things by reference, such as "all seven as recommended" or "both as proposed". Such an entry holds a label: what was recommended stayed in a conversation, so a later reader cannot tell what was decided. The phrase "as recommended" alone is not enough to tell: on the first repository it matched eight lines, seven of which said the decision in the same sentence, and this shape matched the one that did not. The doctor warns of each such line of the records, outside quotation marks; an empty pattern turns the mark and the warning off.

outsidePathsWhy: An instruction file that names a session's scratch folder, a temp folder, a home folder or a memory note by its file points at something no other contributor and no other machine can see.
writeToRepositoriesWhy: Read from the .claude/bowline.json of a folder of repositories: whether bowline writes into the repositories under it. true, the default, lets init --each, move and autosplit write into each one; false keeps every file bowline writes in the folder, for repositories you cannot or would rather not write into; a list of names allows those only. A repository's own file cannot change it, because the choice belongs to the person who works from the folder.
